title: Melchizedek and the Priest Who Lives Forever
summary: The author finally explains Melchizedek, the king of Salem and priest of God Most High who blessed Abraham and received a tenth from him. Because Abraham, and in a sense Levi within him, honored Melchizedek, his priesthood is greater than the Levitical one. Psalm 110:4 promises a new priest in Melchizedek's order, which means the old priesthood and the law tied to it could not bring perfection. Jesus, from the tribe of Judah, is that priest, appointed by God's oath, living forever, able to save completely, and offering himself once for all.
story: Twice already the author has quoted Psalm 110:4 (5:6, 6:20) and promised an explanation, only to interrupt himself with a warning. Now he delivers. The chapter is the theological center of the letter's argument about priesthood. It answers a problem any Jewish reader would raise: Jesus came from the tribe of Judah, not from Levi, so how can he be a priest at all? The answer is that Scripture itself foresaw a different kind of priesthood, older than Aaron's and greater than it. This chapter lays the foundation for chapters 8-10, which describe what this priest does: the covenant he mediates, the sanctuary he enters, and the sacrifice he offers.
historical:
Melchizedek appears only twice in the Old Testament. In Genesis 14:17-20, after Abraham defeated a coalition of kings who had captured his nephew Lot, Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High (El Elyon in Hebrew), brought out bread and wine, blessed Abraham, and received a tenth of the spoils. Salem is usually identified with Jerusalem, which Psalm 76:2 calls by that name. The second mention is Psalm 110:4, a royal psalm in which God swears that the king is a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek, perhaps reflecting David's capture of Jerusalem and the idea that its king inherited an ancient royal priesthood.

Melchizedek fascinated Jewish interpreters in the period of Hebrews. A fragmentary Dead Sea Scroll known as 11QMelchizedek portrays him as a heavenly figure who brings liberation and executes God's judgment at the end of days. Philo of Alexandria read him allegorically as a picture of right reason or the divine word. Later rabbinic tradition sometimes identified him with Shem, the son of Noah. Hebrews takes a different path: it builds its argument from what Genesis says, and from what it does not say, about him.
cultural:
Priesthood in Israel depended on descent. Priests had to prove their ancestry from Aaron, and Ezra 2:62 records men excluded from the priesthood because they could not find their genealogical records. A priest without a genealogy was unthinkable. That is why verse 3 is so striking: Genesis gives Melchizedek no father, no mother, no genealogy, no record of birth or death. The author does not necessarily claim that Melchizedek had no parents; he reads the silence of Scripture as meaningful, a style of argument known in Jewish interpretation, in which what the text omits can also teach. The priest who appears in Scripture without beginning or end is a fitting portrait of the Son, who truly has an indestructible life.

The tithe, a tenth of produce or spoils, was paid to the Levitical priests under the law of Moses (Numbers 18:21-26). Giving a tithe acknowledged the receiver's superior status, and blessing was given by the greater to the lesser (verse 7). Ancient thinking also treated descendants as present in their ancestor, so that Levi could be said to have paid tithes through Abraham (verses 9-10).
literary: The chapter is a close reading of two texts, Genesis 14:17-20 and Psalm 110:4, in four movements. Verses 1-10 retell Genesis 14, interpret Melchizedek's name and title (king of righteousness, king of peace), and argue his superiority to Abraham and Levi. Verses 11-19 use Psalm 110:4 to show that a change of priesthood implies a change of law, since the law was bound up with the Levitical system. Verses 20-25 focus on the oath in the psalm ("The Lord has sworn and will not change His mind"), and on the word forever, contrasting the many mortal priests with the one who lives forever. Verses 26-28 are a hymn-like summary describing Jesus as holy, innocent, undefiled, and exalted, who offered himself once. Key words repeat: perfection, forever, oath, and better.

outline.t: A new priesthood means a new law and a better hope
A priesthood confirmed by God's oath
A permanent priest who always lives to intercede
The high priest we need, who offered himself once

doctrines.note: Jesus is the promised king-priest of Psalm 110, uniting the royal line of Judah with a priesthood that Aaron's line could not provide. In him the offices of king and priest, kept apart in Israel's law, come together.

The Levitical priesthood and the law given through it were God's gift, but they "made nothing perfect" (verse 19). A change of priesthood brings a change of law. The law is not dismissed as evil but recognized as preparatory and fulfilled in Christ.
Jesus "sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself" (verse 27). Priest and sacrifice are the same person, and the offering needs no repeating.
Because Jesus "always lives to intercede", he is able to save completely those who come to God through him (verse 25). The security of believers rests on his permanent, living priesthood.

words.note: Melchisedek, Melchizedek. The Hebrew name combines melek (king) and tsedeq (righteousness), and the author notes the meaning, king of righteousness, and adds that king of Salem means king of peace, since Salem is related to shalom. Righteousness and peace were both expected marks of the messianic reign.

Hierosune, priesthood, the office and institution of priests. Verse 12 makes the chapter's boldest claim: when the priesthood is changed, the law must be changed too, because the Mosaic law and the Levitical priesthood stand or fall together.

Enguos, guarantor or surety, a legal term for someone who pledges himself to make good another's obligation. It appears only here in the New Testament. Jesus is the guarantee of a better covenant (verse 22): he personally stands behind its promises.

Entugchano, to intercede, to approach someone on behalf of another. Jesus always lives to intercede (verse 25). His priestly work did not end at the cross; he continues to represent his people before God, as Romans 8:34 also says.

christ: Christ is the priest-king whom Psalm 110 promised and whom Melchizedek foreshadowed. Unlike the Levitical priests, he holds office not by ancestry but "by the power of an indestructible life" (verse 16), by virtue of his resurrection. His appointment rests on God's oath, so it can never be revoked. He does not die and pass the office on; he "lives forever" and therefore saves completely. He does not offer daily sacrifices for his own sins, since he is "holy, innocent, undefiled", and he offered not an animal but himself, once for all. Melchizedek is a shadow: a priest without recorded beginning or end. Jesus is the substance: a priest who truly lives forever.

hard.q: Who was Melchizedek, really, and is Hebrews claiming he had no parents?
hard.a:
Readers have held several views. Most scholars take Melchizedek to have been a historical Canaanite king of Jerusalem who worshiped the Most High God, and read Hebrews as arguing typologically from the way Genesis presents him. On this view, verse 3 does not claim he literally lacked parents; it notes that Scripture records none, and treats that silence as a picture of an eternal priesthood. The phrase "like the Son of God" (verse 3) supports this reading: Melchizedek resembles the Son, not the other way around. A second view, held by some ancient and modern Christians, identifies Melchizedek as a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ. Its defenders point to the mysterious language of verse 3, but critics reply that Hebrews says he was made like the Son, which suggests he is a distinct figure. A third view, found in some Jewish sources, identified him with Shem, which would give him a genealogy after all. A fourth, suggested by some scholars in light of the Dead Sea Scrolls, sees him as an angelic figure, though Hebrews has already shown the Son to be far above the angels.

What unites these views is the chapter's main point. The priesthood of Jesus rests not on descent but on the power of an indestructible life, confirmed by God's oath. Whoever Melchizedek was, he stands in Scripture as a sign that God had always intended a priesthood greater than Aaron's.

questions: The law made nothing perfect, the author says, but introduced a better hope. What is the difference between trying to be perfect and having a hope by which we draw near to God?
Jesus always lives to intercede for his people. How would it change your prayers and your sense of failure to believe that someone is always praying for you?
Melchizedek appears briefly in Genesis and becomes central here. What does that suggest about how the Bible's small details may carry large significance?
